title: Functional Cache Grafting: Robust and Rapid Code-Policy Synthesis for Embodied Agents
one_liner: Reuse validated function fragments and their cached prompt states so that new control programs can be assembled faster and with fewer code mistakes.
lead: Embodied agents often rely on code-writing models that must regenerate long control programs from scratch for each task. FCGraft stores validated function skeletons together with their cached internal prompt states, retrieves the most relevant functions for a new task, stitches those cached states together, and patches only the small task-specific parts so that synthesis is both faster and more reliable.

problem.h2: Why code-policy generation is slow and error-prone
paras: A code-writing model for an embodied task must read a long prompt, reason about the environment constraints, and write executable control code. That is expensive because prompt processing is repeated for each task, even when many functions are reused across tasks.

Generation is also fragile because full free-form decoding can produce wrong API calls, missing safety checks, or broken control flow. FCGraft reduces both problems by reusing previously validated function pieces and the cached internal states associated with them.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Retrieve validated function fragments and reuse their cached prompt states so that only the task-specific gaps need fresh decoding.

panels.title: 1. A new task arrives
panels.viz_args: The agent needs a fresh control program from a natural-language goal
panels.caption: Starting from scratch repeats a large amount of already solved work.

panels.title: 2. Full regeneration repeats long prompt processing
panels.caption: Full decoding is slow and mistakes appear because everything is regenerated.

panels.title: 3. Retrieve validated functions
panels.viz_args: Find prior code skeletons that match the new task
panels.caption: Reusable code pieces come with cached states from earlier validated prompts.

panels.title: 4. Stitch caches and patch small gaps
panels.viz_args: Compose cached segments, then decode only the missing task-specific parts
panels.caption: Most of the code path is reused, so decoding work and failure risk both drop.

panels.title: 5. A faster, safer policy is produced
panels.caption: The final program is assembled from validated structure plus small targeted edits.

steps.b: Build a library of validated functions
steps.text: Store function-level code skeletons that already execute correctly along with the prompt caches produced when they were generated.

steps.b: Retrieve relevant functions for a new task
steps.text: Choose code fragments whose behavior matches the requested embodied task so that synthesis begins from proven structure.
Combine the stored key-value caches from the retrieved fragments so that the model can resume decoding from a partially prepared internal state.
Decode small task-specific edits for numeric settings, constraints, or environment details because the shared control logic is already present.
Execute the assembled program so that the agent gains both lower latency and higher task success from reused validated structure.

paras: The paper changes code-policy synthesis from full-program generation into retrieval plus partial regeneration.

hidden.name: How much of the new policy can be reused safely
paras: When a new embodied task arrives, the system does not directly know which parts of earlier programs remain valid and which parts need task-specific modification. Reusing too little wastes time, while reusing too much can copy the wrong assumptions.
FCGraft resolves that hidden tradeoff by retrieving function-level matches and patching only the regions that differ. That helps because validated structure is preserved wherever reuse is safe.

heat.caption: Darker means that code region or cache segment is judged more reusable or more important to task success.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is which pieces of an old program are safe to reuse for the new task.
The method retrieves validated functional structure and reuses cached internal states so that only genuinely new code must be decoded.

mechanism.h2: Why this works: keep the validated parts, regenerate only the differences
paras: Latency falls because a large share of prompt processing has already been paid for in the stored caches. Reusing those cached states avoids repeating the full prefill for common functions.

Task success rises because many control bugs come from regenerating standard routines that were already correct before. Function-level reuse preserves safety checks and API structure, while local patching changes only the parts that must adapt to the new task.

stages.s: Stitch stored caches into a composite state

math.h2: Reuse most of the program, decode only the remainder
math.words: A compact summary is that total generation cost equals reused cached cost plus fresh patching cost. The method improves speed when the fresh patching cost is much smaller than writing the full program from scratch.
symbols: overall computation needed to synthesize the policy
cost of retrieving and composing validated cached fragments

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a policy needs four functions.
Three functions are retrieved from the library and stitched with cost 2 each, for reuse cost 6.
One task-specific branch is newly decoded with cost 3.
If full regeneration would cost 20, grafting wins because most of the program was already validated and cached.

math.note: The real system measures speed through cached internal prompt states, but this equation captures the paper's central tradeoff between reuse and fresh decoding.

charts.title: Full code generation or prompt-level caching
charts.note: These approaches trail because they either regenerate too much code or reuse context too coarsely to preserve validated control structure.

charts.title: Functional cache grafting
charts.note: Function-level cache reuse performs better because it preserves proven routines and limits fresh decoding to the parts that actually differ. The values are illustrative summaries of the reported trend.

items.b: The library may not cover the new task well.
items.html: If no validated functions are close to the requested policy, retrieval gives weak building blocks, so patching may expand until the system loses the speed advantage.

items.b: Wrong retrieval can preserve the wrong assumptions.
items.html: A retrieved function may look similar but encode incompatible API usage or control logic, which can hurt execution because the reused skeleton itself is mismatched.
If the system patches too small a region, hidden dependencies can remain stale, and if it patches too much, the method drifts back toward full regeneration.
The paper is useful because it treats synthesis as structured reuse, which reduces both repeated computation and repeated coding errors.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build an embodied-code benchmark with several related household tasks that share navigation, grasp, and safety routines. Compare full generation, prompt-level cache reuse, and function-level cache grafting. For each task, log retrieved functions, patch regions, synthesis time, and execution success.

The demo should show that function-level grafting reaches similar or better execution quality with less decoding because validated code structure is reused directly. Include tasks that require small numeric-setting changes and tasks that require one new branch so that the limits of grafting are visible.
demo.closing: The demo must prove that function-level cache reuse improves embodied code synthesis because most tasks share validated control structure that does not need to be regenerated.
